claim: Treatment of primary human endothelial cells with pro-inflammatory cytokines upregulated cholesterol biosynthetic gene expression within the late phase of the acute inflammatory response.
source: Treatment of primary human ECs with pro-inflammatory cytokines upregulated SREBP2 cleavage and cholesterol biosynthetic gene expression within the late phase of the acute inflammatory response.
evidence: RNA-seq data in Figure 1 shows upregulation of cholesterol biosynthesis pathway genes, and qPCR data in Figure 2b shows increased expression of LDLR, HMGCR, and HMGCS1 at 6-10 hr.

claim: SREBP2 activation in endothelial cells was dependent on NF-κB DNA binding.
source: Furthermore, SREBP2 activation was dependent on NF-κB DNA binding and canonical SCAP-SREBP2 processing.
evidence: Figure 3 shows that RELA knockdown and BAY11-7082 (NF-κB inhibitor) both prevent SREBP2 activation by TNFα.

claim: SREBP2 activation in endothelial cells was dependent on canonical SCAP-SREBP2 processing.
source: Furthermore, SREBP2 activation was dependent on NF-κB DNA binding and canonical SCAP-SREBP2 processing.
evidence: Figure 4 demonstrates that SCAP knockdown, cholesterol supplementation, 25HC, and PF-429242 (S1P inhibitor) all prevent TNFα-induced SREBP2 activation.

claim: Inflammatory activation of SREBP was mediated by a reduction in accessible cholesterol.
source: Mechanistically, inflammatory activation of SREBP was mediated by a reduction in accessible cholesterol, leading to heightened sterol sensing and downstream SREBP2 cleavage.
evidence: Figure 5 shows that TNFα treatment significantly decreased ALOD4 binding (a measure of accessible cholesterol) in cultured HUVECs and in lung endothelial cells from LPS-treated mice.

claim: STARD10 is a novel RELA-inducible target gene.
source: Detailed analysis of NF-κB inducible genes that may impact sterol sensing resulted in the identification of a novel RELA-inducible target, STARD10, that mediates accessible cholesterol homeostasis in ECs.
evidence: Figure 6 shows RNA-seq data indicating STARD10 upregulation by TNFα that is inhibited by RELA knockdown, and ChIP-seq data showing RELA occupancy at the STARD10 promoter.

claim: STARD10 mediates accessible cholesterol homeostasis in endothelial cells.
source: Detailed analysis of NF-κB inducible genes that may impact sterol sensing resulted in the identification of a novel RELA-inducible target, STARD10, that mediates accessible cholesterol homeostasis in ECs.
evidence: Figure 6e shows that STARD10 knockdown significantly rescued the loss in accessible cholesterol caused by TNFα stimulation and attenuated SREBP2 activation.

claim: Endothelial cells rapidly respond to extrinsic signals such as tissue damage or microbial infection by upregulating factors to activate and recruit circulating leukocytes.
source: Endothelial cells (ECs) rapidly respond to extrinsic signals, such as tissue damage or microbial infection, by upregulating factors to activate and recruit circulating leukocytes to the site of injury and aberrant activation of ECs leads to inflammatory based diseases, such as multiple sclerosis and atherosclerosis.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in vascular biology supported by the introduction's discussion of EC inflammatory responses.

claim: Aberrant activation of endothelial cells leads to inflammatory based diseases such as multiple sclerosis and atherosclerosis.
source: Endothelial cells (ECs) rapidly respond to extrinsic signals, such as tissue damage or microbial infection, by upregulating factors to activate and recruit circulating leukocytes to the site of injury and aberrant activation of ECs leads to inflammatory based diseases, such as multiple sclerosis and atherosclerosis.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, consistent with the discussion of EC dysfunction in disease.

claim: TNFα treatment of HUVEC for 10 hr resulted in significant upregulation of 913 genes.
source: Treatment of HUVEC for 10 hr with TNFα resulted in significant upregulation of 913 genes and downregulation of 2202 genes (p<0.05; −1.5>Fold Change (F.C)>1.5) (Figure 1a)
evidence: RNA-seq data analysis with specific statistical cutoffs as shown in Figure 1a volcano plot.

claim: TNFα treatment of HUVEC for 10 hr resulted in significant downregulation of 2202 genes.
source: Treatment of HUVEC for 10 hr with TNFα resulted in significant upregulation of 913 genes and downregulation of 2202 genes (p<0.05; −1.5>Fold Change (F.C)>1.5) (Figure 1a)
evidence: RNA-seq data analysis with specific statistical cutoffs as shown in Figure 1a volcano plot.

claim: RELA knockdown decreased expression of 1067 genes in TNFα-treated HUVEC.
source: RELA knockdown decreased expression of 1067 genes and increased expression of 1112 genes (Figure 1b).
evidence: RNA-seq data from RELA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1b.

claim: RELA knockdown increased expression of 1112 genes in TNFα-treated HUVEC.
source: RELA knockdown decreased expression of 1067 genes and increased expression of 1112 genes (Figure 1b).
evidence: RNA-seq data from RELA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The 'Superpathway of Cholesterol Biosynthesis' was the second most significant pathway upregulated in HUVEC after 10 hr TNFα treatment.
source: Interestingly, Canonical Pathway Analysis uncovered the 'Superpathway of Cholesterol Biosynthesis' as the second most significant pathway upregulated in the 10 hr treatment group.
evidence: IPA analysis results shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Upstream Regulator analysis predicted that SREBF1 was significantly activated in HUVEC treated with TNFα for 10 hr.
source: Furthermore, Upstream Regulator analysis restricted to transcription factors predicted that SREBF1 was significantly activated in these cells.
evidence: IPA upstream regulator analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: SREBP2 cleavage began as early as 6 hr after TNFα treatment and peaked at 10 hr.
source: Measurement of SREBP2(C) throughout a 16 hr timecourse revealed that SREBP2 cleavage began as early as 6 hr after TNFα treatment and peaked at 10 hr (Figure 2a).
evidence: Western blot timecourse data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: SREBP2 activation was dose-dependently induced by TNFα in HUVEC cultured in fetal bovine serum.
source: Furthermore, SREBP2 activation was dose-dependently induced by TNFα in HUVEC cultured in either sterol-sufficient fetal bovine serum (FBS) or in lipoprotein depleted serum (LPDS) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Western blot data showing dose-response in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: SREBP2 activation was dose-dependently induced by TNFα in HUVEC cultured in lipoprotein depleted serum.
source: Furthermore, SREBP2 activation was dose-dependently induced by TNFα in HUVEC cultured in either sterol-sufficient fetal bovine serum (FBS) or in lipoprotein depleted serum (LPDS) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Western blot data showing dose-response in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Known EC NF-κB target genes such as ICAM1, SELE, and CXCL1 were quickly and robustly induced within 2 hr TNFα treatment.
source: Known EC NF-κB target genes, such as ICAM1, SELE, and CXCL1 were quickly and robustly induced within 2 hr TNFα treatment, consistent with the notion that RNA polymerase II is primed at the promoters of these genes to elicit a rapid transcriptional response (Figure 2b, top) (Adelman et al., 2009).
evidence: qRT-PCR timecourse data in Figure 2b and citation to Adelman et al., 2009.

claim: RNA polymerase II is primed at the promoters of NF-κB target genes to elicit a rapid transcriptional response.
source: Known EC NF-κB target genes, such as ICAM1, SELE, and CXCL1 were quickly and robustly induced within 2 hr TNFα treatment, consistent with the notion that RNA polymerase II is primed at the promoters of these genes to elicit a rapid transcriptional response (Figure 2b, top) (Adelman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adelman et al., 2009 and is consistent with the observed rapid induction of NF-κB target genes.

claim: Canonical SREBP2 genes including LDLR, HMGCR, and HMGCS1 significantly increased as early as 6 hr after TNFα treatment and peaked at around 8-10 hr.
source: A majority of the canonical SREBP2 genes, including LDLR, HMGCR, and HMGCS1 significantly increased as early as 6 hr after treatment and peaked at around 8–10 hr (Figure 2b, bottom).
evidence: qRT-PCR timecourse data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Fatty acid synthesis genes known to be SREBP1-dependent such as ACACA/B, FASN, and GPAM did not significantly increase with TNFα treatment.
source: Unlike a majority of the cholesterol biosynthesis genes, several fatty acid synthesis genes known to be SREBP1-dependent, such as ACACA/B, FASN, and GPAM did not significantly increase with TNFα treatment and were unaffected by RELA knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: RNA-seq heatmap data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: TNFα significantly increased LDLR levels in HUVEC cultured in both LPDS and LPDS+LDL.
source: LDL treatment decreased LDLR protein levels in HUVEC at rest and TNFα significantly increased LDLR levels in HUVEC cultured in both LPDS and LPDS +LDL.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2c showing LDLR protein levels under different conditions.

claim: Exogenous LDL was able to partially suppress LDLR expression in TNFα-treated HUVEC.
source: Exogenous LDL was also able to partially suppress LDLR expression, indicating that this process is sterol-sensitive.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2c showing reduced LDLR levels with LDL supplementation.

claim: TNFα treatment led to increased DiI-LDL uptake into cells pre-incubated in various degrees of sterol enriched media.
source: Similar to what was seen by immunoblotting, TNFα treatment led to increased DiI-LDL uptake into cells pre-incubated in various degrees of sterol enriched media (Figure 2d).
evidence: Flow cytometry data measuring DiI-LDL uptake shown in Figure 2d.

claim: TNFα activates I-κ-kinase which phosphorylates and degrades inhibitory IκBα and releases NF-κB to the nucleus.
source: Inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) and interleukin-1 beta (IL1β), bind to their respective receptors to activate I-κ-kinase, which phosphorylates and degrades inhibitory IκBα and releases the key inflammatory transcription factor, NF-κB, to the nucleus (DiDonato et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation to DiDonato et al., 1997.

claim: Treatment of HUVEC with TNFα, IL1β, and lipopolysaccharide to activate NF-κB through separate pathways led to an increase in SREBP2 cleavage.
source: Treatment of HUVEC with TNFα, IL1β, and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to activate NF-κB through separate pathways led to an increase in SREBP2 cleavage and upregulation of LDLR levels (Figure 3a)
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3a showing SREBP2 cleavage with different inflammatory stimuli.

claim: Treatment of HUVEC with TNFα, IL1β, and lipopolysaccharide to activate NF-κB through separate pathways led to upregulation of LDLR levels.
source: Treatment of HUVEC with TNFα, IL1β, and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to activate NF-κB through separate pathways led to an increase in SREBP2 cleavage and upregulation of LDLR levels (Figure 3a)
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3a showing LDLR protein levels with different inflammatory stimuli.

claim: Pre-treatment of HUVEC with actinomycin D blunted activation of SREBP2 in response to TNFα.
source: Furthermore, pre-treatment of HUVEC with the transcription inhibitor, Actinomycin D (ActD), blunted activation of SREBP2, LDLR and ICAM1 in response to TNFα (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3b and quantification in Figure 3c showing reduced SREBP2 activation with ActD.

claim: The mechanism by which inflammatory cytokines activate SREBP2 is most likely through the transcription of novel regulatory molecules rather than via post-translational modifications.
source: This indicated that the mechanism by which inflammatory cytokines activate SREBP2 is most likely through the transcription of novel regulatory molecules rather than via post-translational modifications and/or processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the actinomycin D experiments showing that transcription inhibition blocks SREBP2 activation.

claim: Treatment of HUVEC with BAY 11-7082 significantly attenuated IL1β and TNFα induced increase in SREBP2 cleavage.
source: Treatment of HUVEC with BAY 11–7082, a selective IKK inhibitor, significantly attenuated IL1β and TNFα induced increase in SREBP2 cleavage, LDLR protein levels, and mRNA expression of SREBP2-dependent genes (Figure 3d and e; Keller et al., 2000).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3d showing reduced SREBP2 cleavage with BAY 11-7082 treatment.

claim: BAY 11-7082 is a selective IKK inhibitor.
source: Treatment of HUVEC with BAY 11–7082, a selective IKK inhibitor, significantly attenuated IL1β and TNFα induced increase in SREBP2 cleavage, LDLR protein levels, and mRNA expression of SREBP2-dependent genes (Figure 3d and e; Keller et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keller et al., 2000.

claim: BAY 11-7082 did not suppress JNK or p38 signaling, demonstrating specificity for the NF-κB pathway.
source: Notably, BAY 11–7082 did not suppress JNK or p38 signaling, demonstrating specificity for the NF-κB pathway (Figure 3d).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3d showing maintained JNK and p38 phosphorylation with BAY 11-7082.

claim: RELA knockdown confirmed that NF-κB DNA-binding and transcriptional activity are required for cytokine induction of SREBP2 cleavage.
source: Western Blot analysis of SREBP2 in HUVEC after RELA knockdown confirmed that NF-κB DNA-binding and transcriptional activity are required for cytokine induction of SREBP2 cleavage (Figure 3f).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3f showing reduced SREBP2 cleavage with RELA knockdown.

claim: SREBP2 cleavage can be controlled by mechanisms beyond the SCAP shuttling complex, such as Akt/mTOR/Lipin1 regulation of nuclear SREBP and direct cleavage of SREBP in the ER by S1P.
source: Studies have shown that SREBP2 cleavage can be controlled by mechanisms beyond the SCAP shuttling complex, such as Akt/mTOR/Lipin1 regulation of nuclear SREBP and direct cleavage of SREBP in the ER by S1P (Shimano and Sato, 2017; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shimano and Sato, 2017 and Kim et al., 2018.

claim: Treatment with cholesterol significantly attenuated the increased LDLR and SREBP2 cleavage seen with TNFα stimulation.
source: Chol significantly attenuated the increased LDLR and SREBP2 cleavage seen with TNFα stimulation (Figure 4b).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 4b showing reduced SREBP2 activation with cholesterol supplementation.

claim: LDL was able to dose-dependently decrease SREBP2 activation back down to basal levels at the highest concentration of 250 μg/mL.
source: Furthermore, LDL was able to dose-dependently decrease SREBP2 activation back down to basal levels at the highest concentration of 250 μg/mL (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 4c showing dose-dependent suppression of SREBP2 by LDL.

claim: siRNA knockdown of SCAP inhibited the ability of IL1β and TNFα to upregulate SREBP2 cleavage.
source: To solidify this point, siRNA knockdown of SCAP inhibited the ability of IL1β and TNFα to upregulate SREBP2 cleavage, but not ICAM1 induction (Figure 4d).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 4d showing reduced SREBP2 cleavage with SCAP knockdown.

claim: siRNA knockdown of SCAP did not inhibit ICAM1 induction by IL1β and TNFα.
source: To solidify this point, siRNA knockdown of SCAP inhibited the ability of IL1β and TNFα to upregulate SREBP2 cleavage, but not ICAM1 induction (Figure 4d).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 4d showing maintained ICAM1 induction with SCAP knockdown.

claim: 25-hydroxycholesterol promotes association of INSIG to the SCAP/SREBP2 complex and prevents translocation to the Golgi.
source: The oxysterol 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC) will promote association of INSIG to the SCAP/SREBP2 complex and prevent translocation to the Golgi (Radhakrishnan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2007.

claim: Treatment of HUVEC with 25HC significantly prevented cytokine-induced SREBP2 activation and LDLR upregulation.
source: Treatment of HUVEC with 25HC significantly prevented cytokine-induced SREBP2 activation and LDLR upregulation (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 4e showing suppression of SREBP2 activation by 25HC.

claim: PF-429242 is a potent inhibitor of site-1-protease (S1P).
source: We next treated the cells with PF-429242, a potent inhibitor of site-1-protease (S1P), which prevented SREBP2 cleavage and LDLR increase throughout the 24 hr timecourse (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 d).
evidence: This is stated as a known property of PF-429242 and demonstrated by the experimental results.

claim: PF-429242 prevented SREBP2 cleavage and LDLR increase throughout a 24 hr timecourse.
source: We next treated the cells with PF-429242, a potent inhibitor of site-1-protease (S1P), which prevented SREBP2 cleavage and LDLR increase throughout the 24 hr timecourse (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 d).
evidence: Western blot timecourse data in Figure 4f showing sustained suppression of SREBP2 by PF-429242.

claim: Canonical SCAP shuttling is necessary for activation of SREBP2 by inflammatory cytokines.
source: Taken together, the evidence suggests that canonical SCAP shuttling is necessary for activation of SREBP2 by inflammatory cytokines and that this is not due to direct NF-κB-mediated upregulation of the SREBF2 transcript or cholesterol biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the collective data showing that SCAP inhibition, cholesterol supplementation, and S1P inhibition all block TNFα-induced SREBP2 activation.

claim: TNFα-induced SREBP2 activation is not due to direct NF-κB-mediated upregulation of the SREBF2 transcript.
source: Taken together, the evidence suggests that canonical SCAP shuttling is necessary for activation of SREBP2 by inflammatory cytokines and that this is not due to direct NF-κB-mediated upregulation of the SREBF2 transcript or cholesterol biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SREBP2 activation can be blocked by cholesterol supplementation and SCAP inhibition, indicating sterol-sensing rather than direct transcriptional activation.

claim: TNFα treatment did not alter total cholesterol in HUVEC cultured in LPDS.
source: However, TNFα treatment did not alter total cholesterol in either media condition.
evidence: Cholesterol measurement data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: TNFα treatment did not alter total cholesterol in HUVEC cultured in FBS.
source: However, TNFα treatment did not alter total cholesterol in either media condition.
evidence: Cholesterol measurement data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: TNFα did not change total cholesterol after 4 or 10 hr of treatment as measured by mass spectrometry.
source: Similar to the initial cholesterol measurements, TNFα did not change total cholesterol after 4 or 10 hr of treatment (Figure 5b).
evidence: Mass spectrometry-based lipid analysis data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: TNFα treatment of HUVEC significantly decreased ALOD4 binding.
source: TNFα treatment of HUVEC significantly decreased ALOD4 binding (Figure 5c).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 5c showing reduced ALOD4 binding after TNFα treatment.

claim: Treatment with PF-429242 to reduce SREBP2 processing decreased ALOD4 basally.
source: Using In-Cell Western blotting, treatment with PF-429242 to reduce SREBP2 processing and its transcription decreased ALOD4 basally and, when combined with TNFα, significantly decreased accessible cholesterol even further (Figure 5d).
evidence: In-cell Western blot data in Figure 5d showing reduced ALOD4 binding with PF-429242.

claim: The decrease in accessible cholesterol was independent of SREBP2 stability.
source: This suggests that the decrease in accessible cholesterol was independent of SREBP2 stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PF-429242 (which blocks SREBP2 processing) did not prevent the TNFα-induced decrease in accessible cholesterol.

claim: ALOD4 binding significantly decreased as early as 4 hr after TNFα treatment in HUVEC.
source: Probing accessible cholesterol throughout an 8 hr timecourse revealed that ALOD4 binding significantly decreased as early as 4 hr after TNFα treatment in HUVEC treated with and without PF-429242 (Figure 5e).
evidence: In-cell Western blot timecourse data in Figure 5e.

claim: RELA knockdown attenuated the decrease in accessible cholesterol caused by TNFα.
source: Moreover, RELA knockdown attenuated the decrease in accessible cholesterol, indicating that SREBP2 activation by NF-κB was most likely through upregulation of a molecule or pathway that decreases accessible cholesterol (Figure 5f).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 5f showing maintained ALOD4 binding with RELA knockdown.

claim: Cd31+ endothelial cells from mice treated with LPS contained about 20% less accessible cholesterol compared to ECs from untreated mice.
source: Cd31 +ECs from mice treated with LPS contained about 20% less accessible cholesterol compared to ECs from untreated mice (Figure 5h and i).
evidence: Flow cytometry data from mouse lung endothelial cells shown in Figure 5h and i.

claim: Total serum cholesterol remained unchanged in LPS-treated animals compared to control.
source: Notably, total serum cholesterol remained unchanged in TNFα-treated animals compared to control, indicating that the decrease in accessible cholesterol reflects the effect of the inflammatory stimulus on ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Serum cholesterol measurement data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1h.

claim: TNFα did not impact cholesterol efflux in endothelial cells.
source: Briefly, cholesterol efflux, sphingomyelin shielding, esterification, and lysosomal/endosomal accumulation remained unchanged in ECs treated with TNFα (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cholesterol efflux assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e.

claim: TNFα did not impact sphingomyelin shielding in endothelial cells.
source: Briefly, cholesterol efflux, sphingomyelin shielding, esterification, and lysosomal/endosomal accumulation remained unchanged in ECs treated with TNFα (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Sphingomyelin measurement and OlyA binding data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and d.

claim: TNFα did not impact cholesterol esterification in endothelial cells.
source: Briefly, cholesterol efflux, sphingomyelin shielding, esterification, and lysosomal/endosomal accumulation remained unchanged in ECs treated with TNFα (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Thin layer chromatography data and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: TNFα did not impact lysosomal/endosomal cholesterol accumulation in endothelial cells.
source: Briefly, cholesterol efflux, sphingomyelin shielding, esterification, and lysosomal/endosomal accumulation remained unchanged in ECs treated with TNFα (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: U18666A and chloroquine treatment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f and g.

claim: ABCG1, STARD10, DBI, and NCEH1 have increased RELA occupancy within their promoters upon inflammatory stimulation.
source: We analyzed previously submitted RELA chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) sequencing data of ECs treated with IL1β or TNFα to identify gene candidates that were direct targets of NF-κB (Hogan et al., 2017). Of these genes, ABCG1, STARD10, DBI, and NCEH1 appeared to have increased RELA occupancy within their promoters upon inflammatory stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: ChIP-seq data analysis from Hogan et al., 2017 shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ABCG1 protein levels drastically increased in ECs treated with TNFα.
source: Indeed, ABCG1 protein levels drastically increased in ECs treated with TNFα, which was attenuated by chemical inhibition of NF-κB (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Knockdown of ABCG1 by two independent siRNA were unable to rescue the effect of TNFα on accessible cholesterol.
source: However, knockdown of ABCG1 by two independent siRNA were unable to rescue the effect of TNFα on accessible cholesterol or SREBP2 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3b and c).
evidence: Western blot and qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3b and c.

claim: STARD10 belongs to a family of proteins that bind hydrophobic lipids via a structurally conserved steroidogenic acute regulatory-related lipid transfer (START) domain.
source: STARD10 belongs to a family of proteins that bind hydrophobic lipids via a structurally conserved steroidogenic acute regulatory-related lipid transfer (START) domain (Clark, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Clark, 2020.

claim: STARD proteins regulate non-vesicular trafficking of cholesterol, phospholipids, and sphingolipids between membranes.
source: STARD proteins regulate non-vesicular trafficking of cholesterol, phospholipids, and sphingolipids between membranes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about STARD protein family function.

claim: STARD10 was upregulated by TNFα after 4 and 10 hr of treatment and inhibited by loss of RELA.
source: STARD10 was found to be upregulated by TNFα after 4 and 10 hr of treatment and inhibited by loss of RELA (Figure 6a).
evidence: RNA-seq heatmap data in Figure 6a.

claim: STARD4 is a sterol-sensitive gene.
source: STARD4 also shared this expression pattern, however, it is a sterol-sensitive gene and its upregulation by TNFα most likely occurred via SREBP2 activation (Soccio et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soccio et al., 2005.

claim: RELA chromatin ChIP-seq data revealed increased occupancy of RELA within the STARD10 promoter in ECs treated with IL1β or TNFα.
source: Analysis of RELA chromatin ChIP-seq data revealed increased occupancy of RELA within the STARD10 promoter in ECs treated with IL1β or TNFα (Figure 6b).
evidence: ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: STARD10 was significantly upregulated by TNFα and its expression was dependent on RELA.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed what was indicated by the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq results, revealing that STARD10 was significantly upregulated by TNFα and its expression was dependent on RELA (Figure 6c).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6c.

claim: STARD10 has been shown to bind phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and phosphatidylinositol (PI).
source: STARD10 has been shown to bind phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and phosphatidylinositol (PI), but much of its detailed biology remains unknown (Olayioye et al., 2005; Carrat et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olayioye et al., 2005 and Carrat et al., 2020.

claim: Treatment of ECs with two independent siRNAs targeting STARD10 significantly decreased STARD10 expression.
source: Treatment of ECs with two independent siRNAs targeting STARD10 significantly decreased STARD10 expression and attenuated the enhanced expression of SREBP2 target genes HMGCS1, HMGCR, and LDLR (Figure 6d).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 6d showing reduced STARD10 mRNA with siRNA treatment.

claim: STARD10 knockdown attenuated the enhanced expression of SREBP2 target genes HMGCS1, HMGCR, and LDLR.
source: Treatment of ECs with two independent siRNAs targeting STARD10 significantly decreased STARD10 expression and attenuated the enhanced expression of SREBP2 target genes HMGCS1, HMGCR, and LDLR (Figure 6d).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 6d showing reduced expression of SREBP2 target genes with STARD10 knockdown.

claim: STARD10 knockdown significantly rescued the loss in accessible cholesterol that occurs with TNFα stimulation.
source: Furthermore, STARD10 knockdown significantly rescued the loss in accessible cholesterol that occurs with TNFα stimulation (Figure 6e).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6e showing maintained ALOD4 binding with STARD10 knockdown.

claim: STARD10 knockdown attenuated SREBP2 activation and LDLR upregulation in response to TNFα.
source: SREBP2 activation and LDLR upregulation were also attenuated with STARD10 silencing.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6e showing reduced SREBP2 cleavage and LDLR levels with STARD10 knockdown.

claim: At sufficient cellular cholesterol levels, SREBP is retained as a full-length protein in the endoplasmic reticulum bound to adaptor proteins SCAP and INSIG.
source: At sufficient cellular cholesterol levels, SREBP is retained as a full-length protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) bound to adaptor proteins SREBP cleavage-activating protein (SCAP) and inhibitory insulin-induced gene (INSIG) (Brown and Goldstein, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1997.

claim: When cellular cholesterol levels decrease, the SCAP-SREBP complex translocates to the Golgi where SREBP is proteolytically cleaved by proteases S1P and S2P.
source: When cellular cholesterol levels decrease, the SCAP-SREBP complex translocates to the Golgi where SREBP is proteolytically cleaved by proteases, S1P and S2P.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field describing the canonical SREBP processing pathway.

claim: SREBP1a and SREBP1c isoforms predominantly activate the expression of genes involved in fatty acid synthesis.
source: SREBP1a and SREBP1c isoforms predominantly activate the expression of genes involved in fatty acid synthesis and the SREBP2 isoform upregulates genes that increase cellular cholesterol by de novo synthesis and exogenous uptake (Horton et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Horton et al., 2002.

claim: The SREBP2 isoform upregulates genes that increase cellular cholesterol by de novo synthesis and exogenous uptake.
source: SREBP1a and SREBP1c isoforms predominantly activate the expression of genes involved in fatty acid synthesis and the SREBP2 isoform upregulates genes that increase cellular cholesterol by de novo synthesis and exogenous uptake (Horton et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Horton et al., 2002.

claim: The SCAP/SREBP2 shuttling complex directly interacts with the NLRP3 inflammasome and regulates inflammasome activation via translocation from ER to Golgi in macrophages.
source: In macrophages, it was found that the SCAP/SREBP2 shuttling complex directly interacts with the NLRP3 inflammasome and regulates inflammasome activation via translocation from ER to Golgi (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2018.

claim: SREBP2 was highly activated in macrophages treated with TNFα and nuclear SREBP2 bound to inflammatory and interferon response target genes to promote an M1-like inflammatory state.
source: Another group found that SREBP2 was highly activated in macrophages treated with TNFα and that nuclear SREBP2 bound to inflammatory and interferon response target genes to promote an M1-like inflammatory state (Kusnadi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kusnadi et al., 2019.

claim: Type I interferon signaling in macrophages decreases cholesterol synthesis, allowing for activation of STING on the ER to enhance IFN signaling.
source: Type I interferon (IFN) signaling in macrophages decreases cholesterol synthesis, allowing for activation of STING on the ER to feed forward and enhance IFN signaling (York et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to York et al., 2015.

claim: Decreasing cholesterol synthesis via Srebf2 knockout was sufficient to activate the type I IFN response in macrophages.
source: Furthermore, decreasing cholesterol synthesis via Srebf2 knockout was sufficient to activate the type I IFN response.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the York et al., 2015 study discussed in the previous sentence.

claim: Patients lacking mevalonate kinase accumulate mevalonate and develop hyper immunoglobulin D syndrome.
source: Patients lacking mevalonate kinase accumulate mevalonate and develop hyper immunoglobulin D syndrome (Bekkering et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekkering et al., 2018.

claim: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide or type I IFNs can actively suppress synthesis of cholesterol in macrophages.
source: On the other hand, studies have indicated that bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or type I IFNs can actively suppress synthesis of cholesterol in macrophages and that restoring cholesterol biosynthesis promotes inflammation (Araldi et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araldi et al., 2017 and Dang et al., 2017.

claim: Restoring cholesterol biosynthesis in macrophages promotes inflammation.
source: On the other hand, studies have indicated that bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or type I IFNs can actively suppress synthesis of cholesterol in macrophages and that restoring cholesterol biosynthesis promotes inflammation (Araldi et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araldi et al., 2017 and Dang et al., 2017.

claim: Increased activation of SREBP2 and cholesterol loading in ECs are pro-inflammatory.
source: There is evidence that increased activation of SREBP2 and cholesterol loading in ECs are pro-inflammatory, but these studies were largely focused on models of atherosclerosis and did not focus on the mechanism of activation, flux of the discrete pools of cholesterol and/or sterol sensing in ECs (Xiao et al., 2013; Westerterp et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2013 and Westerterp et al., 2016.

claim: The vascular endothelium is a primary sensor of the circulating bloodstream and is exposed to various stimuli that regulate systemic host defense responses.
source: Indeed, the vascular endothelium is a primary sensor of the circulating bloodstream and is exposed to various stimuli that regulate systemic host defense responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about endothelial cell function.
